The ggelato package provides interactive graphics for exploring hierarchical and grouped time series. Plots are specified with a layered grammar in the style of ggplot2. A plot starts with `gig()`, which holds the data and the aesthetic mapping, and further components are added with `+`.

* A geom layer chooses the view. `geom_features()` draws a feature space, `geom_stl()` draws an STL decomposition and `geom_sunburst()` draws the aggregation structure.
* `hierarchy()` declares the aggregation structure, using the same notation as `fabletools::aggregate_key()`.
* `gig_aes()` maps columns of the data to the channels read by the geom layer.

Every plot carries a hierarchy widget, which displays the levels of the aggregation structure. Levels can be reordered by dragging and switched on or off by clicking, and the series at a chosen level can be filtered by value. A toolbar on each plot provides box and lasso selection, several selection modes, label control and a reset button.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
library(ggelato)
library(fabletools)
library(feasts)
library(tsibble)
```

## Data

The `aus_tourism` data contain quarterly overnight trips from 1998 Q1 to 2022 Q4 for the 76 tourism regions of Australia, disaggregated by purpose of travel. Regions are nested within states, and purpose of travel is crossed with both, which gives the grouped structure `(State / Region) * Purpose`.

To keep this vignette small, the examples use the regions of Victoria and Tasmania. The series at every level of the structure are computed with `aggregate_key()`.

```{r}
#| label: data
south_east <- aus_tourism[aus_tourism$State %in% c("Victoria", "Tasmania"), ]

tourism_hts <- south_east |>
  aggregate_key((State / Region) * Purpose, Trips = sum(Trips))
tourism_hts
```

The aggregated series are marked `<aggregated>` in the key columns. The result contains `r n_keys(tourism_hts)` series. These are the total, the 2 states and the 25 regions, each taken over all purposes of travel and for each of the 4 purposes separately.

## Declaring the aggregation structure

The aggregation structure can be supplied to `gig()` through its `structure` argument or added afterwards with `+ hierarchy()`. The two forms below are equivalent.

```{r}
#| label: structure
#| eval: false
gig(data, structure = (State / Region) * Purpose) + geom_features()

gig(data) + geom_features() + hierarchy((State / Region) * Purpose)
```

A `hierarchy()` object can also be created once and added to several plots of the same data.

```{r}
#| label: hierarchy-object
tourism_structure <- hierarchy((State / Region) * Purpose)
tourism_structure
```

## Feature space

The feature-space plot displays each series as one point, positioned by two features of the series. The features are computed with `fabletools::features()`. Here `feat_stl()` gives the strength of trend and seasonality, together with several other features of the STL decomposition.

```{r}
#| label: features
tourism_features <- tourism_hts |>
  features(Trips, feat_stl)

gig(
  tourism_features,
  gig_aes(x = trend_strength, y = seasonal_strength_year)
) +
  geom_features() +
  tourism_structure
```

The `x` and `y` aesthetics set the initial axes. Any other numeric column of the data can be chosen from the menu on either axis. Points are coloured by their level in the aggregation structure, and selecting a node in the hierarchy widget highlights the corresponding series.

## STL decomposition

The STL plot displays the observed series together with its trend, seasonal and remainder components. The components are computed with `feasts::STL()`. The `trend`, `seasonality` and `remainder` aesthetics must be mapped explicitly, so that no component is guessed from a column name.

```{r}
#| label: stl
tourism_stl <- tourism_hts |>
  model(stl = STL(Trips)) |>
  components()

gig(
  tourism_stl,
  gig_aes(
    x = Quarter, y = Trips, trend = trend,
    seasonality = season_year, remainder = remainder
  )
) +
  geom_stl() +
  tourism_structure
```

Series at different levels of the structure differ greatly in scale. The `scaled` argument of `geom_stl()` accepts a second table of components computed from standardised series, and the toolbar then switches between the original and the standardised scale.

```{r}
#| label: stl-scaled
#| eval: false
tourism_stl_scaled <- tourism_hts |>
  group_by_key() |>
  dplyr::mutate(Trips = as.numeric(scale(Trips))) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  model(stl = STL(Trips)) |>
  components()

gig(
  tourism_stl,
  gig_aes(
    x = Quarter, y = Trips, trend = trend,
    seasonality = season_year, remainder = remainder
  )
) +
  geom_stl(scaled = tourism_stl_scaled) +
  tourism_structure
```

## Sunburst

The sunburst displays the aggregation structure itself. Each ring corresponds to one level of the structure, and each segment to one node at that level. Any table that contains the key columns of the aggregated and bottom-level series can be used, such as the table of features computed above.

```{r}
#| label: sunburst
gig(tourism_features) +
  geom_sunburst() +
  tourism_structure
```

Segment labels can be switched off initially with `geom_sunburst(labels = FALSE)` and toggled from the toolbar.

## The hierarchy widget in existing plots

The hierarchy widget can also be added to line plots made with `plotly::ggplotly()` or with highcharter, through `add_hierarchy_plotly()` and `add_hierarchy_hc()` respectively. The plot must identify the key values of each series, as described in the help pages of these functions. The example below adds the widget to a highcharter plot.

```{r}
#| label: highcharter
library(highcharter)

tourism_lines <- data.frame(
  Quarter = as.numeric(as.Date(tourism_hts$Quarter)),
  State = as.character(tourism_hts$State),
  Region = as.character(tourism_hts$Region),
  Purpose = as.character(tourism_hts$Purpose),
  Trips = tourism_hts$Trips
)

highchart() |>
  hc_add_series(
    tourism_lines,
    type = "line",
    hcaes(x = Quarter, y = Trips, group = interaction(State, Region, Purpose))
  ) |>
  add_hierarchy_hc("(State/Region)*Purpose")
```

## Saving plots and using them in Shiny

A `gig` plot is drawn when it is printed. `gig_build()` returns the underlying htmlwidget, which can be saved as a standalone web page with `htmlwidgets::saveWidget()`. Each geom layer has a pair of Shiny functions, such as `geom_featuresOutput()` and `renderGeomFeatures()`.

```{r}
#| label: shiny
#| eval: false
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(geom_featuresOutput("features", height = "600px"))

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$features <- renderGeomFeatures(
    gig(
      tourism_features,
      gig_aes(x = trend_strength, y = seasonal_strength_year)
    ) +
      geom_features() +
      tourism_structure
  )
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

## Coordinating several views

A `gig()` plot contains a single geom layer. Several plots of the same data can be displayed together with the `fridge` package, which arranges them as movable windows that share one hierarchy widget and one selection.
